en: Saṃyutta Nikāya 18.1 (SN 18.1, PTS SN ii 244) 1. First Chapter: The Discourse on the Eye (Cakkhusutta) “Bhikkhus, the eye is impermanent. Whatever is impermanent is suffering. Whatever is suffering is non-self. Whatever is non-self should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. “The ear is impermanent... The nose is impermanent... The tongue is impermanent... The body is impermanent... The mind is impermanent. Whatever is impermanent is suffering. Whatever is suffering is non-self. Whatever is non-self should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. “Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple experiences revulsion toward the eye, revulsion toward the ear, revulsion toward the nose, revulsion toward the tongue, revulsion toward the body, revulsion toward the mind. Experiencing revulsion, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion [his mind] is liberated. When it is liberated there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’”
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

Then the Venerable Rāhula approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Rāhula said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, it would be well if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent,
and resolute. “What do you think, Rāhula,
is the eye permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir.”
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“Is the ear permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
… [as before] … “Is the nose permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
… “Is the tongue permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir. …
“Is the body permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
… “Is the mind permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, Bhante.
“And that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, Bhante.”
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.”
“Seeing thus, Rāhula, the instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye... he becomes disenchanted with the ear...
he becomes disenchanted with the nose... he becomes disenchanted with the tongue... he becomes disenchanted with the body...
he becomes disenchanted with the mind.”
“Through disenchantment, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, the knowledge arises:
‘It is liberated. He understands: ‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
(By this formula, ten discourses are to be composed.)
First.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 18.2 (SN 18.2, PTS SN ii 245) 1.
First Chapter
The Discourse on Form.
At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying there. “What do you think, Rāhula?”
“Are forms permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
… [and so on] … sounds …
Odors … tastes … tangibles …
“Are phenomena permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, Bhante.
… “Seeing thus, Rāhula, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with forms… becomes disenchanted with sounds…”
“He becomes disenchanted with odors... disenchanted with tastes... disenchanted with tangibles... disenchanted with mental phenomena.
Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate...
[as before] ...he understands.”
The Second [Sutta].
Saṁyutta Nikāya 18.3 (SN 18.3, PTS SN ii 246) 1.
First Chapter
The Discourse on Consciousness. At Sāvatthī.
“What do you think, Rāhula?
“Is eye-consciousness permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
… “Ear-consciousness … [and so on] …”
nose-consciousness … tongue-consciousness … body-consciousness …
“Is mind-consciousness permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, Bhante.
… “Seeing thus, Rāhula, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with eye-consciousness … [and so on] … even with ear-consciousness.”
One becomes disenchanted with nose-consciousness; one becomes disenchanted with tongue-consciousness; one becomes disenchanted with body-consciousness;
one becomes disenchanted with mind-consciousness. Through disenchantment, one becomes dispassionate... [and so on]...
“...he understands.
Thus it was said. The third [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 18.4 (SN 18.4, PTS SN ii 246).
1. First Chapter:
The Discourse on Contact. At Sāvatthī, [the Blessed One] was dwelling.
“What do you think, Rāhula, is eye-contact permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, Bhante. …
“Ear-contact … [and so on] … nose-contact … tongue-contact …”
“Is bodily contact … mental contact permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, Bhante. …

“Seeing thus, Rāhula, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with eye-contact … he becomes disenchanted with ear-contact … he becomes disenchanted with nose-contact … he becomes disenchanted with tongue-contact … he becomes disenchanted with body-contact … he becomes disenchanted with mind-contact.”
“Becoming disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate … [as before] … one understands. Thus ends the fourth [sutta].
Saṁyutta Nikāya 18.5 (SN 18.5, PTS SN ii 247) 1.
First Chapter: The Discourse on Feeling (Vedanāsutta)
Staying at Sāvatthī,
[the Blessed One said]: “What do you think, Rāhula,
is feeling born of eye-contact permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
… “Feeling born of ear-contact … feeling born of nose-contact …”
“Is feeling born of tongue-contact … feeling born of body-contact … feeling born of mind-contact permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.

… “Seeing thus, Rāhula, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with feeling born of eye-contact … ear … nose … tongue … body … and he becomes disenchanted even with feeling born of mind-contact … and he understands it as it really is.”
The Fifth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 18.6 (SN 18.6, PTS SN ii 247) 1.
First Chapter
The Discourse on Perception. At Sāvatthī.
“What do you think, Rāhula?”
“Is the perception of forms permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“… Is the perception of sounds …” [and so on].
perception of odors … perception of tastes … perception of tangibles …
“Is the perception of mental phenomena permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
… “Seeing thus, Rāhula, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the perception of forms … and also with the perception of sounds.”

“He becomes disenchanted … he becomes disenchanted with the perception of odors … he becomes disenchanted with the perception of tastes … he becomes disenchanted with the perception of tangibles … he becomes disenchanted with the perception of mental phenomena … [and so on] … he understands.”
Sixth. Saṁyutta Nikāya 18.7 (SN 18.7, PTS SN ii 247) 1.
First Chapter
The Discourse on Volitional Intention.
At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying there. “What do you think, Rāhula?”
“Is volition regarding form permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, Bhante.
“… volition regarding sound …” [and so on].
Volitional intention regarding odors … volitional intention regarding tastes … volitional intention regarding tangibles …
“Is volition regarding mental phenomena permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
… “Seeing thus, Rāhula, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with volition regarding forms … and also with volition regarding sounds.”

He becomes disenchanted … he becomes disenchanted with volition regarding odors … he becomes disenchanted with volition regarding tastes … he becomes disenchanted with volition regarding tangibles … he becomes disenchanted with volition regarding mental phenomena … [and so on] … he understands.”
The Seventh.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 18.8 (SN 18.8, PTS SN ii 248) 1.
First Chapter
The Discourse on Craving.
At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying there. “What do you think, Rāhula?”
“Is craving for forms permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“… Craving for sounds …” [and so on].
craving for odors … craving for tastes … craving for tangibles …
“Is craving for phenomena permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
… “Seeing thus, Rāhula, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with craving for forms … and also with craving for sounds.”
“He becomes disenchanted with craving for odors; he becomes disenchanted with craving for tastes; he becomes disenchanted with craving for tangibles;
he becomes disenchanted with craving for mental phenomena...
[and so on] ...he understands.”
Eighth. Saṃyutta Nikāya 18.9 (SN 18.9, PTS SN ii 248) 1.
First Chapter
The Discourse on the Elements.
At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying. “What do you think, Rāhula?”
“Is the earth element permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, Bhante.
“… the water element …” [and so on].
the fire element … the air element … the space element …
“Is the consciousness element permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
… “Seeing thus, Rāhula, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the earth element … and also with the water element.”
“He becomes disenchanted with the fire element; he becomes disenchanted with the air element; he becomes disenchanted with the space element;
he becomes disenchanted with the consciousness element...
[and so on] ...he understands.”
The Ninth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 18.10 (SN 18.10, PTS SN ii 249) 1.
First Chapter
The Discourse on the Aggregates.
At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying. “What do you think, Rāhula?”
“Is form permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“… Is feeling …” [and so on].
“Is perception … volitional formations … consciousness permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.

… “Seeing thus, Rāhula, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with volitional formations, and disenchanted with consciousness.
Through disenchantment, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’”
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
This is the tenth [sutta]. The First Chapter.
Its summary verse:
Eye, form, and consciousness,
contact, and feeling.
Perception, volition, and craving— these ten,
by way of the aggregates, are the elements.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 18.11 (SN 18.11, PTS SN ii 249).
2. The Second Chapter:
The Discourse on the Eye.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī.

Then the Venerable Rāhula approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As the Venerable Rāhula was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
"What do you think, Rāhula?"
“Is the eye permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”
“It is suffering, venerable sir.
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”
“No, venerable sir.
“The ear … the nose …”
“Is the tongue … the body … the mind permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir.”
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.”

“Seeing thus, Rāhula, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye … he becomes disenchanted with the ear … he becomes disenchanted with the nose … he becomes disenchanted with the tongue … he becomes disenchanted with the body … he becomes disenchanted with the mind.”
“Through disenchantment, one becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, one is liberated. In liberation, the knowledge arises: ‘It is liberated. One understands:
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
(By this formula, ten discourses are to be composed.)
First.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 18.12–20 (SN 18.12, PTS SN ii 250) 2.
Second Chapter (Dutiyavagga)
The Group of Nine Discourses on Form, etc.
At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying. “What do you think, Rāhula?”
“Are forms permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, Bhante. … [and so on] … sounds …
Odors … tastes … tangibles …
Phenomena … “Eye-consciousness … ear-consciousness …”
nose-consciousness … tongue-consciousness … body-consciousness …
Mind-consciousness … Eye-contact … [and so on] … Ear-contact …
nose-contact … tongue-contact … body-contact …
Mind-contact...
feeling born of eye-contact... pe...
feeling born of ear-contact...
Feeling born of nose-contact … feeling born of tongue-contact … feeling born of body-contact …
Feeling born of mind-contact … perception of forms … perception of sounds … [and so forth].
perception of odors … perception of tastes … perception of tangibles …
Perception of mental phenomena … volition regarding forms … pe … volition regarding sounds …
Volitional intention regarding odors … volitional intention regarding tastes … volitional intention regarding tangibles …
Volition regarding mental phenomena (dhammasañcetanā) … craving for forms (rūpataṇhā) … craving for sounds (saddataṇhā) … [and so on].
craving for odors … craving for tastes … craving for tangibles …
Craving for existence … the earth element … the water element … [and so on].
the fire element … the air element … the space element …
The consciousness element….
Form … feeling … [and so on] … perception … volitional formations … consciousness.
“Is perception … volitional formations … consciousness permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, bhante... [as before] ...
‘Seeing thus, Rāhula... one understands:
“there is no further state of being such as this.”’”
The Tenth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 18.21 (SN 18.21, PTS SN ii 252) 2.
Second Chapter.
The Discourse on Underlying Tendencies.
The Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī.

Then the Venerable Rāhula approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Rāhula said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, for one who knows what and sees what do the underlying tendencies of I-making, mine-making, and conceit not arise with regard to this conscious body and all external signs?
“Rāhula, whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle;
inferior or superior; far or near—all form is to be seen as: ‘This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self.’”
‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’—thus one sees this as it really is with correct wisdom.
Whatever feeling there is... whatever perception there is... [and so on].
Whatever formations...
whatever consciousness there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle;
inferior or superior; far or near—all consciousness is "not mine, this I am not."
‘This is not my self’—thus one sees this as it really is with correct wisdom.
It is for one who knows thus and sees thus, Rāhula, that regarding this conscious body and all external signs, there are no underlying tendencies of ‘I-making,’ ‘mine-making,’ or conceit.
Thus ends the eleventh [discourse].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 18.22 (SN 18.22, PTS SN ii 253) 2. Second Chapter: The Section on the Aggregates Apagata Sutta: Departed “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has departed from form, and his mind has no underlying tendency toward form, he does not perceive form as ‘my self. When he does not perceive form as ‘my self,’ he does not cling to anything in the world. Not clinging, he is not agitated. Being unagitated, he personally attains Nibbāna. He understands: ‘Birth has been destroyed; the holy life has been lived; what had to be done has been done; there is no more coming to any state of being. “When a bhikkhu has departed from feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness, and his mind has no underlying tendency toward consciousness, he does not perceive consciousness as ‘my self. When he does not perceive consciousness as ‘my self,’ he does not cling to anything in the world. Not clinging, he is not agitated. Being unagitated, he personally attains Nibbāna. He understands: ‘Birth has been destroyed; the holy life has been lived; what had to be done has been done; there is no more coming to any state of being.’”
The setting was at Sāvatthī.

Then the Venerable Rāhula approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Rāhula said this to the Blessed One:
“In what way, Bhante, for one who knows how and sees how, regarding this body with consciousness and externally...”
"And how, Rāhula, does the mind become free from the notions of 'I' and 'mine,' devoid of the conceit of 'I am,' transcending all diversity, peaceful, and well-liberated from all signs?
"Rāhula, whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle;
inferior or superior; far or near—all form is to be seen as: 'This is not mine..."
‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’—having seen this thus as it really is with correct wisdom, one is liberated through non-clinging.
Whatever feeling there is... whatever perception there is... [and so on].
Whatever formations...
whatever consciousness, whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle;
inferior or superior; far or near—all consciousness is "not mine, this I am not."
‘This is not my self’—having seen this thus as it really is with correct wisdom, one is liberated through non-clinging.

It is for one who knows thus and sees thus, Rāhula, that the mind becomes free from the notions of ‘I-making’ and ‘my-making’ regarding both this conscious body and all external signs; it transcends all diversification, and being peaceful, it is well-liberated.
(The Twelfth)
The Second Chapter.
Its summary (uddāna) is:
The eye, form, and consciousness;
Contact and feeling;
perception, volition, and craving—
these ten, by way of elements, constitute the aggregates.
Because the underlying tendency has been removed,
it is therefore called a "chapter.
The *Rāhula Saṃyutta* is complete.
